knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 3.3.1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly defines null vs alternative, Type I vs Type II error, p-value, and power?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Keep Type I/II in the reject-true-null / fail-to-reject-false-null directions. A p-value is a tail probability under H₀, not P(H₀|data) and not P(H₁). Power is P(reject H₀ | H₁ true).
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Null vs alternative; Type I = false reject; Type II = false retain; p-value = extreme-tail probability under H₀; power = P(reject | H₁).
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Swapping Type I/II, or reading the p-value as P(H₀|data) or P(H₁).

choices.label: The null is the statement under test; the alternative is the competing claim. Type I error is rejecting a true null; Type II error is failing to reject a false null. A p-value is the probability, under the null, of a result at least as extreme as observed; power is the probability of rejecting a false null.
Type I error is failing to reject a false null; Type II error is rejecting a true null. A p-value is the probability that the alternative is true.
A p-value is the probability that the null is true given the data, and power is one minus the p-value.
Null and alternative are interchangeable labels; only the test statistic formula matters, not which hypothesis is labelled null.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 3.3.1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Disease screening: H₀ = no disease, H₁ = disease present. Which statement is correct?
knowledge_checks.body: HT vocabulary on a vignette; refuse cookbook-test-as-concepts.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: In this framing, false positive = Type I and false negative = Type II. p-value and power keep their usual frequentist meanings. Software theatre does not replace the concepts.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Type I = false positive; Type II = false negative; p-value under H₀; power = 1−β; concepts ≠ cookbook click.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Swapping Type I/II, or treating a software z-test as the concepts.

choices.label: Type I error is a false positive (declare disease when healthy). Type II error is a false negative (miss disease when present). A p-value is the probability under H₀ of a result at least as extreme as observed; power is P(reject H₀ | H₁ true). Running a software z-test does not by itself replace this vocabulary.
Type I error is missing disease when it is present; Type II error is declaring disease when healthy.
A p-value is the probability of having the disease, and power is the probability of not having the disease.
Because a one-sample Normal mean test can be clicked in software, Type I/II, p-value, and power definitions are unnecessary.

worked_example.title: Two-sided p-value for a claim-mean z-test
worked_example.problem_statement: A pricing team tests H₀: μ = £10,000 vs H₁: μ ≠ £10,000 for mean claim cost at significance level α = 0.05. The test statistic is z = 2.1 under H₀ (standard Normal). Compute the two-sided p-value and state the decision. Use Φ(2.1) = 0.9821.
worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Write the two-sided p-value as 2[1 − Φ(|z|)] before substituting.

steps.label: Upper-tail probability
steps.explanation: For a continuous symmetric null, the one-sided tail is 1 − Φ(|z|).

steps.label: Two-sided p-value
steps.explanation: A two-sided alternative charges both tails; the p-value is twice the one-sided tail probability.

steps.label: Decision at α = 0.05
steps.explanation: Reject H₀ when p ≤ α. Here p = 0.0358 < 0.05.

worked_example.final_answer: Two-sided p-value = 0.0358; reject H₀: μ = £10,000 at α = 0.05.
worked_example.common_pitfall: Reporting only the one-sided tail 0.0179 as the p-value for a two-sided alternative, or comparing z to α directly (2.1 vs 0.05).
